AC9M5N01.title: Decimals beyond hundredths
AC9M5N01.lead: Read, compare and locate decimals by naming the value of each digit, including thousandths.
AC9M5N01.before: Know tenths and hundredths, whole-number place value and equal number-line intervals.

focuses.title: Name each decimal place
focuses.explain: Each place to the right is one tenth of the place before it. One hundredth is ten thousandths. The whole must stay the same when a model is subdivided.
focuses.example: Read 4.307 using place value.
steps: 4 ones + 3 tenths + 0 hundredths + 7 thousandths.
The 7 is worth 0.007, not 0.07. Say “four point three zero seven”.
focuses.watch: A zero inside the numeral holds a place; 4.307 and 4.037 are different.
focuses.tryit: What is the value of 8 in 2.086?
focuses.answer: Eight hundredths: 0.08.

focuses.title: Rename without changing the amount
focuses.explain: Splitting a unit makes more, smaller pieces of the same amount. Appending a zero after the final decimal digit changes its name, not its value.
steps: Four tenths are forty hundredths or four hundred thousandths.
To divide 0.4 by ten, share 40 hundredths into ten equal groups: 4 hundredths = 0.04.
focuses.watch: Dividing by ten makes the amount smaller; do not just erase or add a zero.
focuses.tryit: Write 0.7 ÷ 10.
focuses.answer: 0.07; seven tenths shared into ten groups gives seven hundredths.

focuses.title: Compare and order using common places
focuses.explain: Compare the ones first, then tenths, hundredths and thousandths until the first difference. Trailing zeros can help align the places.
steps: Ones and tenths agree. At hundredths, 0 < 8, so 2.508 < 2.58 = 2.580.
focuses.watch: More decimal digits do not automatically mean a larger number.
focuses.tryit: Which is larger: 1.709 kg or 1.79 kg?
focuses.answer: 1.79 kg = 1.790 kg; nine hundredths is greater than zero hundredths.

focuses.title: Locate a decimal between close endpoints
focuses.explain: Zoom in on a number line. Ten equal intervals from 2.33 to 2.34 are thousandths because the total gap is one hundredth.
focuses.example: Locate 2.335.
steps: The left endpoint is 2.330 and the right is 2.340.
2.335 is five thousandths after 2.330, halfway through the interval.
focuses.watch: Count intervals, not tick marks. A diagram of a length needs its unit as well as its number.
focuses.tryit: Where is 2.338 between these endpoints?
focuses.answer: Eight of the ten equal intervals after 2.330; it is closer to 2.34.

AC9M5N02.title: Factors, multiples and divisibility
AC9M5N02.lead: Build factor pairs, recognise multiples and explain why a number divides exactly.
AC9M5N02.before: Recall multiplication facts and distinguish a whole group from a remainder.

focuses.title: Build all the factor pairs
focuses.explain: A factor divides a positive whole number exactly. Arrays connect the factors to the number of rows and the number in each row.
focuses.example: Find the factors of 24.
steps: Arrange 24 counters as 1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8 and 4 × 6.
Check candidate row sizes systematically. After 4, 5 fails and 6 repeats the 4 × 6 pair.
List both numbers from every pair: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24.
focuses.watch: Listing only small factors misses their partners. Square pairs such as 6 × 6 contribute the factor 6 once.
focuses.tryit: List the factor pairs of 18.

focuses.title: Generate and combine multiples
focuses.explain: A positive multiple is a number multiplied by 1, 2, 3 and so on. Equal groups can be split without changing their total.
focuses.example: Build multiples of 7 from groups of 5 and 2.
steps: Combine 4 × 5 = 20 and 4 × 2 = 8: the total is 28.
The first five positive multiples are 7, 14, 21, 28, 35.
focuses.watch: A factor belongs to the number’s factor set; its multiples continue without a last positive multiple.
focuses.tryit: Use groups of 5 and 2 to find 6 × 7.

focuses.title: Explain tests for 2, 5 and 10
focuses.explain: Base-ten groups explain the last-digit tests. Every full ten can be split into pairs or groups of five, so the ones decide whether anything is left over.
focuses.example: Is 340 divisible by 2, 5 and 10?
steps: The ones digit 0 leaves no extra ones after its 34 tens.
It is even, ends in 0 or 5, and ends in 0: all three tests pass.
focuses.watch: A divisibility test means no remainder, not merely a close answer.
focuses.tryit: Which of 2, 5 and 10 divide 135?
focuses.answer: Only 5. The last digit is odd and is not zero.

focuses.title: Use digit sums and check the result
focuses.explain: For 3 and 9, sum the digits. Each ten is one more than a multiple of 9, so replacing tens by ones leaves the same remainder for these tests.
focuses.example: Test 4 572 for divisibility by 3 and 9.
steps: 4 + 5 + 7 + 2 = 18, which is divisible by both 3 and 9.
4 572 = 3 × 1 524 and 9 × 508 confirm both tests.
focuses.watch: The digit-sum rule for 3 or 9 is not a rule for every divisor.
focuses.tryit: Is 2 314 divisible by 3?
focuses.answer: No: 2 + 3 + 1 + 4 = 10, which is not a multiple of 3.

AC9M5N03.title: Comparing and ordering fractions
AC9M5N03.lead: Use equal-sized wholes, equivalent fractions and number lines to compare fractions and mixed numbers.
AC9M5N03.before: Know equal parts, numerator, denominator and multiplication facts.

focuses.title: Keep the whole and the fractional unit clear
focuses.explain: A fraction wall shows parts of an area or strip. A number line shows a point measured from zero. Equal fractions share a line position when the whole unit is fixed.
focuses.example: Compare 3/8 and 5/8.
steps: Both count eighths of the same whole.
Five of these equal parts are more than three, so 3/8 < 5/8.
focuses.watch: Different-sized source wholes can make a picture comparison misleading.
focuses.tryit: Which is greater: 7/10 or 4/10?
focuses.answer: 7/10, because seven tenths exceed four tenths.

focuses.title: Rename related denominators
focuses.explain: Use a multiple of the smaller denominator to make the units match. Multiply numerator and denominator by the same number.
focuses.example: Compare 2/3 and 5/6.
steps: Each third splits into two sixths: 2/3 = 4/6.
Compare 4/6 with 5/6: 2/3 < 5/6.
focuses.watch: Changing only the denominator changes the amount.
focuses.tryit: Compare 3/4 and 7/8.

focuses.title: Move between mixed numbers and improper fractions
focuses.explain: An improper fraction can include complete wholes. A mixed number records the complete wholes and the remaining fractional part.
focuses.example: Locate 11/4.
steps: Eight quarters make two wholes; three quarters remain.
11/4 = 2 3/4, three quarter-steps after 2 and before 3.
focuses.watch: A mixed number such as 2 3/4 means 2 + 3/4, not 2 × 3/4.
focuses.tryit: Write 3 2/5 as an improper fraction.
focuses.answer: 17/5: three wholes are fifteen fifths, then add two fifths.

focuses.title: Order a mixed set and justify the positions
focuses.explain: Compare whole-number parts first. When these match, compare the fractional parts with common units.
steps: Rename in quarters: 6/4, 7/4 and 5/4.
From least to greatest: 1 1/4, 1 1/2, 7/4.
All lie between 1 and 2; 7/4 = 1 3/4 is furthest right.
focuses.watch: Keep the original labels in the final ordered list so the answer matches the question.

AC9M5N04.title: Percentages, fractions and decimals
AC9M5N04.lead: Treat one complete whole as 100%, then connect familiar proportions and compare their relative size.
AC9M5N04.before: Recognise halves, quarters, tenths and hundredths of a stated whole.

focuses.title: Identify the whole and show percent
focuses.explain: Percent means “per hundred”. A complete hundred-cell grid represents 100%; each equal cell represents 1%.
focuses.example: Read a grid with 35 of its 100 cells shaded.
steps: The whole is all 100 cells.
35 shaded cells represent 35/100 = 35%.
The 65 unshaded cells represent 65%; 35% + 65% = 100%.
focuses.watch: Two different-sized complete containers are both 100% full; they need not contain the same amount.
focuses.tryit: If 20% of the original juice is used, what percentage remains?
focuses.answer: 80%, because used and remaining portions make the same original 100%.

focuses.title: Connect familiar fractions to percentages
focuses.explain: Rename a fraction in hundredths, or subdivide a grid into equal groups. The proportion stays the same.
focuses.example: Write 3/4 as a percentage.
steps: Divide 100 cells into four equal groups of 25.
Three groups contain 75 cells: 3/4 = 75/100 = 75%.
focuses.watch: The denominator does not tell you the percentage on its own.
focuses.tryit: Write 2/5 as a percentage.

focuses.title: Connect percentages and decimal place value
focuses.explain: A decimal names parts of one whole. Hundredths link it directly with a percentage.
focuses.example: Connect 0.6, 6/10 and a percentage.
steps: Sixty per hundred is 60%. Similarly, 0.25 = 25% = 1/4.
focuses.watch: 0.05 is 5%, while 0.5 is 50%. The zero matters.
focuses.tryit: Write 75% as a decimal.
focuses.answer: 0.75, because seventy-five per hundred is seventy-five hundredths.

focuses.title: Compare proportions and read everyday claims
focuses.explain: Use a common representation when fractions, decimals and percentages are mixed. A larger proportion does not guarantee a larger actual amount if the wholes differ.
focuses.example: Compare 50%, 0.7 and 3/4.
steps: Write 50%, 70% and 75%.
The order is 50% < 0.7 < 3/4.
On the same device, a 70% indicator represents a greater proportion of capacity than 50%.
focuses.watch: A sale sign saying 25% off describes a proportion of the original price; it does not mean $25 off.
focuses.tryit: Which is the greater proportion: 0.4 or 45%?

AC9M5N05.title: Adding and subtracting fractions
AC9M5N05.lead: Name common fractional units before combining or removing amounts.
AC9M5N05.before: Know equivalent fractions, related denominators and mixed numbers.

focuses.title: Add or remove the same-sized parts
focuses.explain: The denominator names the fractional unit; the numerator counts how many of those units you have.
focuses.example: Work out 5/8 − 2/8.
steps: Remove two eighths from five eighths.
Three eighths remain: 5/8 − 2/8 = 3/8.
For addition, 3/8 + 4/8 = 7/8 uses the same eighth-sized unit.
focuses.watch: Adding denominators would change the size of the parts.
focuses.answer: 6/7: two sevenths plus four sevenths is six sevenths.

focuses.title: Rename related units before calculating
focuses.explain: Split each larger fractional part into smaller equal parts of the same whole. Use strips, a number line or equivalent fractions.
steps: One half is four eighths: 1/2 = 4/8.
A jump of four eighths followed by three eighths reaches seven eighths.
focuses.watch: Only rename when needed: related denominators already have an efficient common unit.

focuses.title: Cross a whole with fractions and mixed numbers
focuses.explain: A whole can be regrouped into fractional parts without changing the total.
focuses.example: Cut 3/4 m from a 2 1/4 m strip.
steps: Rename 2 1/4 m as 1 5/4 m.
Check by adding the cut piece back: 1 1/2 + 3/4 = 2 1/4 m.
focuses.watch: Keep the measurement unit. Equivalent unsimplified fractions are valid unless simplest form is requested.

focuses.title: Choose a model for the situation
focuses.explain: A clock can model fractional hours, a marked strip can model length and a cup can model capacity. The whole and operation must match the context.
focuses.example: Add half an hour and three-quarters of an hour.
steps: Half an hour is two quarters of an hour.
Each quarter-hour is 15 minutes, so this is 75 minutes.
focuses.watch: “Subtract a from b” means b − a. Do not automatically subtract in the order the quantities appear.
focuses.tryit: A recipe uses 3/4 cup, then another 1/4 cup. What is the total?
focuses.answer: One cup: four quarters make one whole cup.

AC9M5N06.title: Multiplying larger numbers
AC9M5N06.lead: Choose a useful multiplication strategy, connect it to place value and check the size of the answer.
AC9M5N06.before: Recall multiplication facts and partition whole numbers into hundreds, tens and ones.

focuses.title: Use doubling and factor regrouping
focuses.explain: Multiplying by four is doubling twice. Reordering and regrouping factors can make a product easier without changing it.
focuses.example: Find 246 × 4.
steps: Double again: 492 × 2 = 984.
focuses.watch: Doubling both original factors makes the product four times as large.
focuses.tryit: Use doubling to find 132 × 4.

focuses.title: Partition every place-value contribution
focuses.explain: An area model splits a product into smaller rectangles. Each partial product must be included exactly once.
focuses.example: Find 324 × 8.
steps: Add the contributions: 2 400 + 160 + 32 = 2 592.
These are the same place-value contributions combined by a written multiplication algorithm.
focuses.watch: A tens digit represents tens, not ones.
focuses.tryit: Find 213 × 6 using partial products.

focuses.title: Multiply by a two-digit number
focuses.explain: Split the two-digit factor into tens and ones. Written rows record those two contributions.
steps: 146 × 20 = 2 920, because twenty means two tens.
focuses.watch: The tens row is 2 920, not 292; its place-value shift is essential.
focuses.tryit: Work out 125 × 12.

focuses.title: Choose efficiency and check with an estimate
focuses.explain: Number features suggest a strategy. Compensation adjusts the full amount added by a convenient change. Use a calculator when the context makes it useful, after predicting the scale.
focuses.example: Find the cost of 7 items at $198 each.
steps: The convenient price adds $2 for each of seven items, so subtract $14: total $1 386.
The estimate about $1 400 makes $13 860 implausible; it does not prove every digit is correct.
focuses.watch: State whether you are giving an estimate or the exact product.
focuses.tryit: Use compensation to find 6 × 49.

AC9M5N07.title: Division and remainders
AC9M5N07.lead: Choose an efficient division method, then decide what the remainder means in the situation.
AC9M5N07.before: Use multiplication facts, place value and equal sharing/grouping.

focuses.title: Use multiplication to reason about division
focuses.explain: A division asks for a group size or a number of groups. The related multiplication checks the result.
focuses.example: Find 84 ÷ 7.
steps: Ask how many sevens make 84.
Ten sevens make 70; two more make 14.
There are 12 sevens, so 84 ÷ 7 = 12.
focuses.watch: The dividend is the total; the divisor gives the group size or group count.
focuses.tryit: Find 96 ÷ 8.
focuses.answer: 12, checked by 12 × 8 = 96.

focuses.title: Partition or scale both numbers
focuses.explain: Split a dividend into convenient multiples, or divide both dividend and divisor by the same nonzero factor to preserve the quotient.
focuses.example: Find 468 ÷ 6.
steps: Add the group counts: 70 + 8 = 78.
For 240 ÷ 20, divide both numbers by 10 to get 24 ÷ 2 = 12.
focuses.watch: Dividing only one number by ten changes the quotient.
focuses.tryit: Simplify 360 ÷ 30 by scaling both numbers.

focuses.title: Round the group count in the right direction
focuses.explain: A remainder cannot be ignored until the practical question is answered. Full containers, enough seats and shared lengths need different interpretations.
focuses.example: Transport 127 people in vehicles seating 20 each.
steps: 127 ÷ 20 = 6 remainder 7.
Six vehicles seat only 120, so seven people still need seats.
Seven vehicles are needed. For complete packs of 20 made from 127 objects, only six complete packs can be filled.
focuses.watch: The same quotient can require rounding up, rounding down or keeping a fraction, depending on the context.
focuses.tryit: How many 8-seat vehicles are needed for 35 people?
focuses.answer: Five; four vehicles seat 32 people and leave three without seats.

focuses.title: Share a remainder as a fraction or decimal
focuses.explain: When the quantity can be subdivided, share the remainder as well. Retain exact fractions when the decimal does not terminate.
focuses.example: Share 17 m equally among four people.
steps: 17 ÷ 4 = 4 remainder 1.
Share the remaining metre into four equal parts: 1/4 m each.
Each receives 4 1/4 m = 4.25 m. Check: 4 × 4.25 = 17.
focuses.watch: A calculator display such as 0.333333 is an approximation to one third, not an exact terminating decimal.
focuses.tryit: Share 13 litres equally into five containers.
focuses.answer: 2 3/5 L = 2.6 L in each container.

AC9M5N08.title: Estimation and reasonableness
AC9M5N08.lead: Choose an estimate that answers the practical question, then explain what it can and cannot establish.
AC9M5N08.before: Round whole numbers and familiar decimal amounts; know the four operations.

focuses.title: Decide whether the answer can be approximate
focuses.explain: An estimate is useful for planning or spotting an implausible answer. An exact payment or an exact number of tickets needs more precision.
focuses.example: Check a claimed cost of $1 450 for 6 items at $24 each.
steps: Use $25 per item: 6 × 25 = 150.
The total should be near $150, so $1 450 is much too high.
The estimate rejects the claim without giving the exact cost.
focuses.watch: A close estimate is not proof of an exact answer.
focuses.tryit: Is 8 × 49 closer to 40, 400 or 4 000?

focuses.title: Use compatible values and explain the choice
focuses.explain: Choose nearby numbers that are easy for the operation. Keep any rounding place specified in the question.
focuses.example: Estimate 398 ÷ 8.
steps: 400 is close to 398 and divisible by 8.
400 ÷ 8 = 50, so the answer is about 50.
Because the dividend was increased and the divisor stayed fixed, this is a little high.
focuses.watch: Rounding both numbers is not always more helpful than changing just one.
focuses.tryit: Estimate 1 198 ÷ 6 using a nearby compatible dividend.
focuses.answer: About 200, using 1 200 ÷ 6.

focuses.title: Track the direction of a rounding change
focuses.explain: For positive numbers, increasing an addend increases a sum; increasing a factor increases a product. For subtraction, increasing the amount removed makes the result smaller.
focuses.example: Compare estimates for 502 − 198.
steps: 500 − 200 = 300: the first amount went down while the amount removed went up, so this estimate is low.
For division, increasing the dividend raises the quotient, while increasing the divisor lowers it.
If both numbers change, inspect the effects; do not assume they cancel.
focuses.watch: Both-up or both-down rounding has no universal direction for differences or quotients.
focuses.tryit: Is 600 − 200 above or below the exact value of 598 − 203?
focuses.answer: Above: the first amount increased and the amount removed decreased.

focuses.title: Use conservative budgets and sensible payment rounding
focuses.explain: Rounding prices upwards gives a cautious shopping budget. This planning choice is different from the final amount charged.
focuses.example: Four items each cost less than $5. Is $20 enough?
steps: Their total is less than 4 × $5 = $20, so $20 is sufficient.
For Australian cash settlement, round the final total to the nearest 5c; a $12.42 total becomes $12.40.
A card payment remains $12.42. Do not round each item as a charging rule.
focuses.watch: An estimate must be labelled as an estimate, not as the receipt total.
focuses.tryit: Three items each cost less than $8. Is $24 enough?
focuses.answer: Yes; their combined cost is less than $24.

AC9M5N09.title: Solving practical problems with models
AC9M5N09.lead: Turn a practical goal into a mathematical plan, calculate, then check and explain the result in context.
AC9M5N09.before: Select addition, subtraction, multiplication or division from equal-group and comparison situations.

focuses.title: State the goal and the missing information
focuses.explain: A model is a mathematical description of a situation. Identify what must be found, relevant quantities, units and constraints before choosing operations.
focuses.example: Plan enough notebooks for 28 students, sold in packs of 6.
steps: Assume each student needs one notebook and no spare notebooks are already available.
4 packs contain only 24; 5 packs contain 30.
The model requires five packs, with two notebooks spare.
focuses.watch: A supplied expression alone does not show how the situation was formulated.
focuses.tryit: What extra information is needed to calculate the purchase cost?
focuses.answer: The price per pack, and whether any delivery or other charges apply.

focuses.title: Represent the relationships and choose operations
focuses.explain: Use an equal-group diagram, bar model, table or number sentence to show why each calculation is needed.
focuses.example: Six groups need 4 markers each; 7 usable markers are already available.
steps: Six groups of four require 6 × 4 = 24 markers.
Subtract the 7 already available: 24 − 7 = 17 more.
The sentence 6 × 4 − 7 = 17 records the situation.
focuses.watch: The word “each” describes a relationship; read the whole problem before choosing an operation.
focuses.tryit: Five tables need six pencils each, with eight pencils already available. How many more?
focuses.answer: 5 × 6 − 8 = 22 more pencils.

focuses.title: Build a budget and use a spreadsheet
focuses.explain: Distinguish sales income, expenses and money remaining after expenses. A spreadsheet can make changing assumptions visible.
focuses.example: A class sells 40 tickets at $3 each and spends $45 on materials.
steps: Net proceeds after materials: $120 − $45 = $75.
In a spreadsheet put ticket count in B2, price in C2 and expenses in D2; =B2*C2-D2 computes net proceeds.
focuses.watch: This model assumes all 40 tickets sell and there are no other costs. A digital calculation still needs a checked model.
focuses.tryit: If only 30 tickets sell with the same price and expenses, what remains?

focuses.title: Validate, communicate and revise
focuses.explain: Check units, arithmetic and whether the answer meets the original goal. Change assumptions when the practical evidence changes.
focuses.example: At $3 per ticket and fixed costs of $45, does selling 40 tickets raise at least $80 after costs?
steps: The original plan gives $75, below the $80 target.
At 42 tickets the net is $126 − $45 = $81; at 41 it is $78.
If capacity allows, 42 ticket sales meet the target under the stated assumptions. Communicate the minimum and the assumptions.
focuses.watch: An open plan may have several valid solutions; justify one rather than claiming it is universally best.
focuses.tryit: What happens to the 42-ticket plan if expenses rise by $5?
focuses.answer: Net proceeds become $76, so the plan no longer meets the $80 target.

AC9M5N10.title: Algorithms for factors and multiples
AC9M5N10.lead: Write clear steps and decisions, test them with digital tools and explain the patterns you find.
AC9M5N10.before: Understand factors, multiples, exact division and multiplication facts.

focuses.title: Make the decision rule explicit
focuses.explain: An algorithm states the input, ordered steps, decisions, output and when to stop. A flowchart shows which branch to follow.
focuses.example: Test whether 126 is divisible by 6.
steps: Add its digits: 1 + 2 + 6 = 9, a multiple of 3.
Its last digit is even, so it is divisible by both 2 and 3.
Output “divisible by 6”. If either test fails, output “not divisible by 6”, then stop.
focuses.watch: For this rule the tests are joined by AND, not OR.
focuses.tryit: Use the algorithm for 123.
focuses.answer: Not divisible by 6: its digit sum is divisible by 3 but it is odd.

focuses.title: Create a systematic factor search
focuses.explain: For a positive input number, test possible divisors in order. If division leaves no remainder, record the divisor and its partner.
focuses.example: Design a search for the factors of 20.
steps: Start a candidate at 1; divide 20 by it. Record 1 and 20.
Increase the candidate by 1 and repeat up to 20, recording exact divisors only.
Remove duplicate entries or store each factor once: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20.
focuses.watch: The process needs a stopping rule. A correct factor guess is not a complete algorithm.
focuses.tryit: What should the algorithm output for input 9?
focuses.answer: 1, 3 and 9, with 3 recorded once.

focuses.title: Generate multiples in a spreadsheet
focuses.explain: Keep the chosen number in one cell and multiply it by a changing whole-number index. Use fill down to repeat the rule.
focuses.example: Make a multiples-of-8 column.
steps: Enter 8 in B1. Put 1, 2, 3, 4 … in A2, A3, A4, A5 …
In B2 enter =$B$1*A2 and fill down. The dollar signs fix B1 while the A-row changes.
The first results are 8, 16, 24, 32 … Change B1 to 6 and check that the whole column updates.
focuses.watch: Reading a supplied column is useful practice; actually creating and changing the spreadsheet is part of this investigation.
focuses.tryit: What is the fifth positive multiple when B1 contains 6?
focuses.answer: 30. Check by creating the column and reading its fifth result.

focuses.title: Compare common values and test a pattern
focuses.explain: A common multiple appears in every list; the least positive one is the LCM. A common factor divides every input; the largest is the HCF.
focuses.example: Compare 6 and 9.
steps: Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18 …; multiples of 9: 9, 18 …; LCM = 18.
Factors of 6: 1, 2, 3, 6; of 9: 1, 3, 9; HCF = 3.
For 3, 4 and 5, the HCF is 1 and the LCM is 60. Extend the spreadsheet far enough to see it.
focuses.watch: A short list can miss the first common multiple; no overlap yet does not mean none exists.
focuses.tryit: Find the LCM and HCF of 4 and 6.
focuses.answer: LCM 12; HCF 2. Test both results against each input.

AC9M5A01.title: Multiplication and division fact families
AC9M5A01.lead: Use one equal-group model to explain related multiplication and division facts.
AC9M5A01.before: Know groups, rows, columns, a total and multiplication facts.

focuses.title: Identify the total and the two factors
focuses.explain: Multiplication combines equal groups. Division can recover the size of a group or the number of groups from that total.
focuses.example: Model 4 groups of 6 counters.
steps: 4 × 6 = 24 gives the total.
24 ÷ 4 = 6 shares that total among four groups.
24 ÷ 6 = 4 asks how many groups of six fit.
focuses.watch: Swapping factors is commutativity; using division to undo multiplication is the inverse relationship.
focuses.tryit: Five groups contain 7 objects each. What division facts match?

focuses.title: Write a connected family of facts
focuses.explain: Turning an array swaps rows and columns while keeping the total. Connect both multiplication orders to their division facts.
focuses.example: Write the family for 3, 8 and 24.
steps: Every statement describes the same 24 objects.
focuses.watch: When the two factors are equal, some statements repeat: 6 × 6 = 36 and 36 ÷ 6 = 6 give only two distinct equations.
focuses.tryit: How many distinct equations are in the 5, 5, 25 fact family?

focuses.title: Use inverse facts to calculate efficiently
focuses.explain: A friendly multiplication can reveal a division without repeated subtraction. Think about the sizes of the groups.
steps: Therefore 240 ÷ 20 = 12.
Check by recombining twelve groups of twenty.
focuses.watch: Do not change the total while switching between related facts.
focuses.tryit: Use 14 × 6 = 84 to find 84 ÷ 14.
focuses.answer: 6, because fourteen groups of six make 84.

focuses.title: Explain halving and the zero boundary
focuses.explain: Halving twice divides into four equal parts. Multiplication checks the shared result. Zero cannot be a divisor.
focuses.example: Find 68 ÷ 4 by halving.
steps: Half of 68 is 34; half of 34 is 17.
Four seventeens make 68, so the answer is 17.
0 × 5 = 0 connects to 0 ÷ 5 = 0, but not to 0 ÷ 0.
focuses.watch: Dividing by zero is undefined; do not manufacture a four-equation family with zero.
focuses.tryit: Use halving twice to find 92 ÷ 4.

AC9M5A02.title: Unknown values in multiplication and division
AC9M5A02.lead: Identify the missing quantity and use inverse operations and number properties to keep equations balanced.
AC9M5A02.before: Know multiplication/division facts and that an equals sign means “has the same value”.

focuses.title: Identify what the missing number represents
focuses.explain: An unknown can be a factor, a total or a divisor. Its position determines the related calculation.
focuses.example: Find the blank in 72 ÷ □ = 8.
steps: The blank is the group size when eight groups make 72.
Use 8 × □ = 72, giving □ = 9.
Substitute: 72 ÷ 9 = 8.
focuses.watch: 72 ÷ □ = 8 and □ ÷ 8 = 72 are different equations.
focuses.tryit: Find □ in □ × 7 = 91.

focuses.title: Use equality as a balance
focuses.explain: Both sides of an equation can contain calculations. Find a value that makes both sides equal rather than treating the equals sign as “write the answer next”.
steps: The left side is 24.
48 ÷ 2 = 24, so the blank is 2.
Check the original equation: both sides have value 24.
focuses.watch: Scaling dividend and divisor together preserves a quotient: 15 ÷ 3 = 30 ÷ 6.

focuses.title: Use order and grouping carefully
focuses.explain: Multiplication permits swapping factors and regrouping them. Division does not generally permit the same changes.
focuses.example: Explain 3 × 8 = 6 × 4.
steps: Replace 8 by 2 × 4.
Compare division: (24 ÷ 6) ÷ 2 = 2, but 24 ÷ (6 ÷ 2) = 8. The grouping matters.
focuses.watch: The multiplication properties are not permission to swap or regroup division at will.
focuses.tryit: Complete 5 × 12 = 10 × □.
focuses.answer: 6: split 12 into 2 × 6 and regroup 5 × 2.

focuses.title: Distribute over parts and check the unknown
focuses.explain: A partitioned array lets you multiply each part and combine the products. This explains the distributive property.
steps: Split 14 into 10 + 4.
7 × 14 = 70 + 28, so the blank is 4.
Both sides equal 98.
focuses.watch: Every part must be multiplied: 7 × (10 + 4) is not 70 + 4.
focuses.answer: 2, because 18 = 20 − 2; both sides equal 108.

AC9M5M01.title: Choosing metric units and measuring accurately
AC9M5M01.lead: Choose a suitable unit and instrument, then use smaller units when the measurement needs finer detail.
AC9M5M01.before: Recognise metres, centimetres, millimetres, grams, kilograms, litres and millilitres.

focuses.title: Match the attribute and the scale of the object
focuses.explain: Length measures distance, mass measures how much matter and capacity measures how much a container can hold. Choose a unit that makes the result useful.
focuses.example: Choose units for a pencil, a schoolbag and a drink bottle.
steps: Centimetres or millimetres suit the pencil’s length.
Kilograms suit the loaded bag’s mass; millilitres suit a small bottle’s capacity.
For length: kilometre > metre > centimetre > millimetre.
focuses.watch: Amount currently in a container is not necessarily its full capacity.
focuses.tryit: Which unit suits the distance between towns: millimetres or kilometres?
focuses.answer: Kilometres; they suit the large distance.

focuses.title: Read intervals and align the instrument
focuses.explain: Check the labelled unit and the size of each interval. Align a ruler’s zero with the start, or subtract the two endpoint readings.
focuses.example: An object starts at 2 cm and ends at 8.4 cm on a ruler.
steps: Its length is the difference, not the final reading.
Read a scale with 10 equal intervals between 100 g and 200 g as 10 g per interval.
focuses.watch: The physical edge of the ruler may not be its zero mark.
focuses.tryit: What is the length from 3 cm to 9.7 cm?
focuses.answer: 6.7 cm, the difference between the endpoints.

focuses.title: Combine units to show finer detail
focuses.explain: A metre contains 100 centimetres; a centimetre contains 10 millimetres. One kilogram is 1 000 grams and one litre is 1 000 millilitres.
focuses.example: Record a jump of 2 m and 37 cm.
steps: The two complete metres are 200 cm.
A mass of 1 kg 80 g similarly means 1 080 g, not 180 g.
focuses.watch: Mixed units cannot simply be joined as digit strings.
focuses.tryit: Write 1 L 250 mL in millilitres.

focuses.title: Measure, compare and explain the needed accuracy
focuses.explain: Use a tool whose graduations suit the job, and repeat a careful measurement. Smaller units can record finer detail; they do not fix poor technique.
focuses.example: Measure a book’s width to decide whether it fits a shelf space.
steps: Estimate its width, then align a ruler correctly.
Read centimetres and remaining millimetres, keeping your viewing angle consistent.
Compare with the actual shelf gap, leaving any required clearance.
focuses.watch: Writing extra decimal digits does not create a more accurate observation.
focuses.tryit: Why might millimetres be useful for a 1 cm-wide shelf clearance?
focuses.answer: They show small differences that whole-centimetre readings can miss; careful alignment is still necessary.

AC9M5M02.title: Perimeter and area of regular and irregular shapes
AC9M5M02.lead: Trace the boundary for perimeter and cover the region for area, using the right units.
AC9M5M02.before: Measure lengths and count equal square units; know rows and columns.

focuses.title: Trace every outside edge
focuses.explain: Perimeter is the total distance around a boundary, including inward turns in an irregular outline. Internal dividing lines are not part of the outside perimeter.
focuses.example: Find the perimeter of a 7 m by 4 m rectangular garden.
steps: Equivalently, double one length plus one width: 2 × (7 + 4) = 22.
A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles; a rectangle need not be regular.
focuses.watch: Perimeter uses length units such as metres, not square metres.
focuses.tryit: What is the perimeter of a 6 cm by 3 cm rectangle?

focuses.title: Cover the inside with square units
focuses.explain: Area measures how much surface is covered. Count equal squares without gaps or overlaps. Rows and columns make counting efficient.
focuses.example: Cover a 7 m by 4 m rectangular floor.
steps: Imagine four rows, each containing seven 1 m² tiles.
There are 4 × 7 = 28 square metres.
The 22 m boundary and 28 m² region are different kinds of measure.
focuses.watch: A bare comparison such as “28 is bigger than 22” does not compare area and perimeter as the same quantity.
focuses.tryit: How many 1 cm² squares cover a 6 cm by 3 cm rectangle?
focuses.answer: 18 squares, so 18 cm².

focuses.title: Split an irregular region or count grid cells
focuses.explain: Decompose a shape into non-overlapping parts, or complete a rectangle and remove a missing region. Count partial squares to estimate curved boundaries.
focuses.example: Find the area of a 6 m by 4 m rectangle with a 2 m by 1 m corner removed.
steps: The complete rectangle contains 24 m².
The missing corner contains 2 m².
The remaining area is 24 − 2 = 22 m².
focuses.watch: Do not count a region twice, and do not assume a dotted partition is a hole.
focuses.tryit: What remains if a 3 m by 2 m corner is removed from an 8 m by 5 m rectangle?

focuses.title: Compare designs for a practical purpose
focuses.explain: The same perimeter can enclose different areas. State whether you are buying boundary material or covering a surface.
focuses.example: Compare 7 m × 4 m and 6 m × 5 m garden beds.
steps: Both perimeters are 22 m.
Their areas are 28 m² and 30 m².
The second provides 2 m² more planting space with the same boundary length. A real design must also allow paths.
focuses.watch: Equal perimeter does not imply equal area.
focuses.tryit: Two 1 m² squares touch along one full side. Find the combined area and perimeter.
focuses.answer: Area 2 m²; perimeter 6 m. The shared side is internal.

AC9M5M03.title: 12-hour and 24-hour time
AC9M5M03.lead: Connect clock faces, AM/PM times and 24-hour timetables, including noon and midnight.
AC9M5M03.before: Read an analogue clock and know that one hour contains 60 minutes.

focuses.title: Match the same time in two systems
focuses.explain: The 12-hour clock repeats twice each day. The 24-hour clock numbers the hours from 00 to 23. Minutes keep the same meaning.
focuses.example: Match 16:30 to a 12-hour time and clock face.
steps: The minute hand is at 6 and the hour hand is halfway between 4 and 5.
The same face could show 4:30 AM; the day period distinguishes them.
focuses.watch: The hour hand moves continuously; at half past it is not exactly on the hour numeral.
focuses.tryit: Write 08:15 in 12-hour time.

focuses.title: Convert in both directions
focuses.explain: For PM hours 1 to 11, add 12 to get 24-hour time. For AM hours 1 to 11, keep the hour and use a leading zero when needed.
focuses.example: Convert 7:45 PM and 21:05.
focuses.watch: Add or subtract 12 hours, not 12 minutes; minutes are not decimal fractions of an hour.
focuses.tryit: Convert 6:08 PM to 24-hour time.

focuses.title: Handle noon and midnight explicitly
focuses.explain: Noon is 12:00 PM or 12:00. Midnight at the start of a stated day is 12:00 AM or 00:00. These are exceptions to a simple “add 12” rule.
focuses.example: Convert 12:20 AM and 12:20 PM.
steps: 12:20 AM is twenty minutes after midnight: 00:20.
12:20 PM is twenty minutes after noon: 12:20.
focuses.watch: 12 AM is midnight; 12 PM is noon. State the day when a journey crosses midnight.
focuses.tryit: What is 00:35 in 12-hour time?

focuses.title: Use a timetable and check the date
focuses.explain: Read the correct service and day, then convert as needed. A clock time is a position in the day; duration is the time between positions.
focuses.example: A bus leaves Monday at 23:40 and arrives Tuesday at 00:15.
steps: Departure is 11:40 PM Monday; arrival is 12:15 AM Tuesday.
There are 20 minutes to midnight and 15 more to arrival.
The journey lasts 35 minutes.
focuses.watch: Subtracting the displayed hours without the day change can produce a meaningless negative duration.
focuses.tryit: A service leaves at 13:25 and arrives at 14:05 on the same day. How long?
focuses.answer: 40 minutes: 35 minutes to 14:00 and 5 more.

AC9M5M04.title: Estimating, measuring and constructing angles
AC9M5M04.lead: Use turn benchmarks, align a protractor and construct a requested angle with a ruler.
AC9M5M04.before: Recognise quarter, half and full turns and a common vertex.

focuses.title: Connect angle names with degree measures
focuses.explain: An angle measures a turn between rays meeting at a vertex. A right angle is 90°, a straight angle 180° and a full turn 360°.
focuses.example: Classify 40°, 125° and 240°.
steps: 40° is acute: greater than 0° and less than 90°.
125° is obtuse: greater than 90° and less than 180°.
240° is reflex: greater than 180° and less than 360°.
focuses.watch: A straight angle and a full turn are not reflex angles. Longer rays do not make a wider angle.
focuses.tryit: Classify 90° and 180°.
focuses.answer: Right angle and straight angle, respectively.

focuses.title: Estimate against familiar turns
focuses.explain: Compare the marked opening with a right angle or half turn before measuring. State whether you mean the smaller or the reflex opening.
focuses.example: Estimate an opening halfway between a right and a straight angle.
steps: 90° is a quarter turn and 180° is a half turn.
Halfway is about 135°, an obtuse angle.
A quarter-turn is not an estimate for an opening visibly wider than a right angle.
focuses.watch: An estimate is approximate; a rough picture alone does not establish an exact measure.
focuses.tryit: A turn is three right angles. How many degrees is it?
focuses.answer: 270°, a three-quarter turn and a reflex angle.

focuses.title: Measure from the correct zero
focuses.explain: Put the protractor centre on the vertex and its baseline on the starting ray. Follow the scale beginning at zero on that ray.
focuses.example: One ray follows the right-hand zero; the other crosses the 50°/130° pair.
steps: Start at the right-hand zero and follow that scale.
It reads 50°, agreeing with an acute opening.
130° belongs to the opposite scale and would describe an obtuse opening.
focuses.watch: Do not always use the inside scale; the starting ray determines the scale.
focuses.tryit: Which reading fits a marked obtuse opening at a 40°/140° pair?
focuses.answer: 140°; verify that this is the scale beginning at the aligned zero.

focuses.title: Construct, then check the intended angle
focuses.explain: A construction needs a chosen vertex, a starting ray, a correctly aligned tool and a second ray drawn through the degree mark.
focuses.example: Construct a 60° angle on paper.
steps: Draw ray AB with a ruler; A is the vertex.
Centre the protractor at A, align its zero with AB and mark 60° on that scale.
Remove the tool and draw a ray from A through the mark. Label the 60° opening and remeasure.
For a reflex 240° angle, construct the smaller 120° opening and mark the outside turn: 360° − 120° = 240°.
focuses.watch: A label alone is not a construction. Changing the starting direction is fine if the requested angle size remains correct.
focuses.tryit: Construct and check 110° on paper.
focuses.answer: The two rays share a vertex and the marked obtuse opening measures 110° with your aligned protractor.

AC9M5SP01.title: Nets and 3D objects
AC9M5SP01.lead: Connect faces to an object, predict folds and build a net that closes correctly.
AC9M5SP01.before: Recognise faces, edges, vertices, prisms and pyramids.

focuses.title: Connect each face to the object
focuses.explain: A net is a connected flat arrangement of faces that folds into a three-dimensional object. Count hidden faces too.
focuses.example: Compare a triangular prism and a square pyramid.
steps: A right triangular prism has two matching triangular ends and three rectangular side faces.
A square pyramid has one square base and four triangles meeting at an apex.
The base is one of the faces, not an additional component.
focuses.watch: Having the correct number of faces is necessary but does not prove that an arrangement will fold.
focuses.tryit: What faces does a cube need?
focuses.answer: Six equal squares.

focuses.title: Track folds and opposite faces
focuses.explain: Faces fold along shared edges. Imagine one face as the base, then lift neighbouring faces one at a time and check for overlap.
focuses.example: Fold the labelled cube cross shown.
steps: Use B as a base. Its neighbours A, C, E and F become four side faces.
D folds over to close the remaining face opposite B.
Opposite pairs are A–C, B–D and E–F. Six squares in one straight row cannot close a cube.
focuses.watch: Faces touching only at a point do not provide an edge to fold along.
focuses.tryit: In this cross, which face is opposite E?
focuses.answer: F; they fold from opposite sides of B.

focuses.title: Sketch, cut, fold and test
focuses.explain: Use compatible edge lengths. Distinguish the outside cut boundary from internal fold lines. Joining tabs help assembly but are not extra faces.
focuses.example: Build a cube from the cross net.
steps: Choose a square side length, such as 3 cm, and draw all six squares to that size.
Add small joining tabs where needed, cut the outside boundary and score or crease the shared edges.
Fold, join and check that every edge closes without overlap or gaps; revise the drawing if it fails.
focuses.watch: An adult can help with safe cutting while the learner makes the spatial decisions.
focuses.tryit: How would you check a proposed net before adding glue?
focuses.answer: Fold it dry, match the free edges and check that every required face is present and closes correctly.

focuses.title: Design packaging for a purpose
focuses.explain: A useful package must fit its contents and have a workable way to open and join. Label the dimensions before constructing it.
focuses.example: Plan a rectangular box for an item 6 cm long, 4 cm wide and 2 cm high.
steps: Use two 6 × 4 faces, two 6 × 2 faces and two 4 × 2 faces as the minimum mathematical face sizes.
Arrange a connected net with matching shared edges; allow practical clearance for the item and material thickness.
Make a paper trial and decide which face becomes the lid.
focuses.watch: A face list is not a finished net; test the arrangement and opening.
focuses.tryit: What must change if a cardboard trial is too tight?
focuses.answer: Increase the relevant inside dimensions or clearance and revise the matching faces and edges together.

AC9M5SP02.title: Grid coordinates and movement
AC9M5SP02.lead: Construct numbered axes, locate exact intersections and describe a route from a stated start.
AC9M5SP02.before: Read equal number-line intervals and distinguish horizontal from vertical.

focuses.title: Construct the coordinate system
focuses.explain: Draw two perpendicular number lines meeting at zero. Number equal intervals on the lines, not the spaces. The shared zero is the origin.
focuses.example: Make a grid from 0 to 6 on each axis.
steps: Draw a horizontal axis and a vertical axis with a shared zero.
Mark each unit the same distance apart along its axis, then extend the grid lines.
A cell reference names an area; a coordinate pair names an exact intersection.
focuses.watch: Letter/number cell references and ordered coordinates are different locating systems.
focuses.tryit: Where is the origin?
focuses.answer: At the shared zero: (0, 0).

focuses.title: Read and plot the horizontal value first
focuses.explain: Write an ordered pair in brackets with a comma. Move along the horizontal axis first, then vertically.
focuses.example: Plot P(2, 4) and Q(4, 2).
steps: P is two units right and four up from the origin.
Q is four right and two up.
The points differ even though they use the same two numbers.
focuses.watch: (5, 0) lies on the horizontal axis; (0, 3) lies on the vertical axis.
focuses.tryit: Which labelled point is two units up and four units right?
focuses.answer: Q(4, 2), because horizontal is written first.

focuses.title: Describe a route from its current position
focuses.explain: Name the start, grid units and direction. Each instruction acts on the latest point.
focuses.example: Start at (2, 1), move three units right, then two up.
steps: Three right changes the horizontal coordinate to 5: (5, 1).
Two up changes the vertical coordinate to 3: (5, 3).
To return, reverse the order and directions: two down, then three left.
focuses.watch: Count spaces between lines, not the number of lines crossed including the start.
focuses.tryit: Start at (5, 4), move two left and three down. Where do you finish?

focuses.title: Communicate and check a drawing
focuses.explain: List vertices in the order they should be joined. A partner needs the same axes, scale and join instructions to reproduce the shape.
focuses.example: Re-create A(1, 1), B(4, 1), C(4, 3), D(1, 3), joining A–B–C–D–A.
steps: Plot each exact intersection and label it.
Join in the stated order to form a rectangle three units wide and two high.
Compare with a partner’s drawing and use the coordinates to locate any disagreement.
focuses.watch: A correct list without joining instructions may not determine the intended picture.
focuses.tryit: How would moving every vertex one unit up change this rectangle?
focuses.answer: Its vertical coordinates all increase by one; its width and height remain the same.

AC9M5SP03.title: Translations, reflections and rotations
AC9M5SP03.lead: Perform and describe shape movements, then test what stays the same and whether the shape has symmetry.
AC9M5SP03.before: Recognise a shape’s vertices, equal lengths and quarter/half turns.

focuses.title: Translate every point by the same move
focuses.explain: A translation slides a shape without turning or flipping it. Every point moves the same distance in the same direction.
focuses.example: Move a triangle three grid units right.
steps: Choose a vertex and count three equal spaces right.
Move each remaining vertex three spaces right, then join corresponding vertices.
Lengths, angles, size and orientation stay the same; position changes.
focuses.watch: Moving different vertices by different amounts distorts the shape instead of translating it.
focuses.tryit: A shape moves two units up. What happens to its side lengths?
focuses.answer: They stay unchanged. Every vertex moves the same two-unit displacement.

focuses.title: Reflect across a stated mirror line
focuses.explain: A reflection flips a shape. Corresponding points lie on opposite sides of the mirror line at equal perpendicular distances.
focuses.example: Reflect the triangle in the vertical dashed line.
steps: For each vertex, count its horizontal distance to this vertical mirror line.
Mark a point the same distance across the line at the same height.
Join the new vertices. The shape is the same size but its orientation is reversed.
focuses.watch: The nearest edge of the drawing is not automatically the mirror line; use the stated line.
focuses.tryit: What happens to a vertex exactly on the mirror line?
focuses.answer: It stays in the same position.

focuses.title: Rotate about a stated centre
focuses.explain: A rotation turns every point around the same centre by a stated amount and direction. Distances from the centre stay fixed.
focuses.example: Turn a paper arrow a quarter-turn clockwise about its tail.
steps: Pin or mark the tail as the centre.
Rotate through 90° clockwise; an arrow initially pointing up now points right.
Keep the centre fixed and trace the image. A further clockwise quarter-turn points down.
focuses.watch: “Rotate 90°” is incomplete if the centre or direction is missing.
focuses.tryit: An up-pointing arrow makes a half-turn about its tail. Which way does it point?
focuses.answer: Down. A half-turn is 180° in either direction.

focuses.title: Compare sequences and test symmetries
focuses.explain: A symmetry maps a shape exactly onto itself. Reflection symmetry uses a mirror line; rotational symmetry uses a turn smaller than 360°.
focuses.example: Test a non-square rectangle.
steps: It has two mirror lines through the midpoints of opposite sides.
A 180° turn about its centre matches it to itself; a 90° turn does not.
Two successive half-turns about the same centre return any shape to its start, as do two reflections in the same line. Use tracing or geometry software to test.
focuses.watch: A transformation and a symmetry are different ideas: a move may produce a new position without matching the original.
focuses.tryit: How many mirror lines does an unmarked square have?
focuses.answer: Four: two through opposite side midpoints and two diagonals. It also matches after 90°, 180° and 270° centre turns.

AC9M5ST01.title: Collecting, displaying and describing data
AC9M5ST01.lead: Choose a variable, check the records and use tables or graphs to explain the distribution.
AC9M5ST01.before: Read a tally, a labelled scale and a simple column graph.

focuses.title: Identify what kind of data is needed
focuses.explain: A variable is the feature recorded. Nominal categories have no natural order; ordinal categories do; discrete numerical data counts things.
focuses.example: Classify a travel survey.
steps: Travel mode (walk, bus, car) is nominal categorical.
Satisfaction (poor, fair, good) is ordinal categorical. Ratings 1–5 can label ordered categories too.
Number of journeys is discrete numerical: it counts whole journeys.
focuses.watch: Number labels do not automatically turn a rating category into a measured quantity.
focuses.tryit: Is the number of pets nominal categorical or discrete numerical?
focuses.answer: Discrete numerical; it counts pets.

focuses.title: Collect and validate the records
focuses.explain: Use consistent categories and one record per intended observation. Check missing values, impossible counts and accidental duplicate entries.
focuses.example: Validate a spreadsheet column for number of pets.
steps: Accept nonnegative whole numbers such as 0, 1 and 2.
Check an entry of −2 or 1.5 against the original response instead of silently using it.
Keep the column in a number format; use an agreed category for missing responses rather than treating them as zero.
focuses.watch: Two people may genuinely give the same answer; equal values are not automatically duplicate records.
focuses.tryit: A blank response is entered as zero pets. Why check it?
focuses.answer: Blank means not recorded; zero states that the person has no pets.

focuses.title: Create a frequency table and suitable graph
focuses.explain: Frequency counts how often a value occurs. A column graph displays category or count frequencies with a consistent scale.
focuses.example: Display these illustrative pet-count records: 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4.
steps: Tally the values: 0→1, 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, 4→1. Frequencies total 8.
Enter values in spreadsheet column A and frequencies in B; select both columns and insert a column chart.
Label the axes “Number of pets” and “Number of respondents”; use a zero-based frequency scale.
focuses.watch: Do not graph the list positions as though they were the pet values.
focuses.tryit: What height should the bar for two pets have?
focuses.answer: 3 respondents.

focuses.title: Describe mode and shape in context
focuses.explain: The mode is the value or category with the highest frequency. For ordered numerical data, discuss where results cluster, spread and have gaps. Nominal category order cannot support a numerical shape claim.
focuses.example: Describe these illustrative pet counts: 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4.
steps: Two pets is the mode, occurring three times. Four is the largest count but not the mode.
Most responses are one or two pets; counts run from zero to four, with fewer at the high end.
In 1, 1, 2, 3, 3 there are two modes: 1 and 3.
focuses.watch: The highest frequency is a count; the mode is the value or category having that frequency.
focuses.tryit: For 0, 1, 1, 2, 4, 4, name all modes.
focuses.answer: 1 and 4; each occurs twice.

AC9M5ST02.title: Interpreting line graphs
AC9M5ST02.lead: Read time and value scales, compare changes and distinguish observations from estimates and predictions.
AC9M5ST02.before: Read labelled axes and subtract to compare measurements.

focuses.title: Read the axes, units and plotted values
focuses.explain: A line graph connects measurements over time. Identify the time unit, quantity unit and intervals before reading a point.
focuses.example: Read the illustrative tank-volume graph.
steps: The horizontal axis is time in hours; the vertical axis is volume in litres.
At 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 hours the plotted volumes are 10, 14, 14, 8 and 12 litres.
The line passes through each labelled observation.
focuses.watch: The graph’s height represents the quantity, not elapsed time.
focuses.tryit: What volume was recorded at 2 hours?
focuses.answer: 14 litres.

focuses.title: Compare changes over equal periods
focuses.explain: Rising sections show increases, falling sections decreases and horizontal sections no change. Compare numerical changes over equal time intervals.
focuses.example: Compare the first three one-hour intervals.
steps: From hour 0 to 1, volume increases by 4 L.
From 1 to 2, it stays at 14 L.
From 2 to 3, it decreases by 6 L: the largest change in magnitude among these intervals.
focuses.watch: A steep-looking line can mislead if axes or time intervals differ; check both scales.
focuses.tryit: How much does the volume increase from hour 3 to 4?

focuses.title: Estimate between observations carefully
focuses.explain: A point on a connecting segment can give an estimate between recorded times. The actual quantity may have changed differently between observations.
focuses.example: Estimate the volume at 3.5 hours.
steps: The segment rises from 8 L at hour 3 to 12 L at hour 4.
Halfway on this straight segment is about 10 L.
This is an estimate, not an additional measured observation.
focuses.watch: A line does not guarantee that real change was constant between the recorded points.
focuses.tryit: Was 10 L at 3.5 hours directly measured in the example?
focuses.answer: No; only whole-hour values were supplied.

focuses.title: Match stories and limit conclusions
focuses.explain: Use a graph’s pattern to support a story, then check whether the labels and context allow the conclusion.
focuses.example: What could explain the tank graph?
steps: An increase could show filling; a level section could show no net change; a decrease could show water leaving.
These are plausible explanations, not proven causes.
The graph stops at 4 hours and does not determine the volume at 10 hours. Predictions from past trends can fail if conditions change.
focuses.watch: A larger final value does not mean the quantity increased throughout.
focuses.tryit: Can you conclude the tank was always filling from hour 0 to 4?
focuses.answer: No. The graph has a constant section and a falling section.

AC9M5ST03.title: Planning a statistical investigation
AC9M5ST03.lead: Ask a useful question, collect relevant data, choose a display and communicate a conclusion with limits.
AC9M5ST03.before: Sort categories, tally counts and interpret a labelled graph.

focuses.title: Pose a question and define the group
focuses.explain: A statistical question anticipates variation. Decide whose answers or which observations are relevant and what each record will mean.
focuses.example: Investigate preferred lunchtime activities in one class.
steps: Ask “Which activity would you most like offered at lunch?”
Define the target as this class and one response per student.
Offer balanced options such as games, reading, drawing, sport and another activity.
focuses.watch: “Don’t you agree sport is best?” leads respondents and does not give a balanced choice.
focuses.tryit: Why define the group before collecting responses?
focuses.answer: It determines who should be included and how far the conclusion can apply.

focuses.title: Plan and collect consistently
focuses.explain: Choose a survey, observation or experiment suited to the question. Set a recording rule, gather the data and check the total.
focuses.example: Conduct the class activity survey.
steps: Ask the same neutral question and offer the same choices to each participant.
Record one choice per person; allow “no preference” or nonresponse to be recorded clearly.
Check that frequency totals match the valid response count. Do not invent missing responses.
focuses.watch: A worked example table is not evidence that you conducted the investigation.
focuses.tryit: Carry out a small survey with an agreed group. What should your record include?
focuses.answer: The question, group, date, method, actual responses, category definitions and any missing responses.

focuses.title: Choose a display that answers the question
focuses.explain: A frequency table or column graph compares category counts. A line graph suits measured change over time, not unordered favourite activities.
focuses.example: Display illustrative results: games 7, reading 4, drawing 5 and sport 8.
steps: The 24 responses can be organised in a frequency table.
Draw four separated equal-width bars with a consistent scale, title and category/count axis labels.
Sport has the most responses, but 16 respondents chose something else.
focuses.watch: The most frequent choice does not necessarily have more than half of the responses.
focuses.tryit: Does sport have a majority of these 24 responses?
focuses.answer: No. Eight is the largest category, but it is less than half of 24.

focuses.title: Interpret, communicate and improve
focuses.explain: Answer the original question using actual evidence. State limitations and a sensible next action; do not generalise beyond the group studied.
focuses.example: Report the illustrative survey.
steps: “Sport was the most selected option in this class: 8 of 24 responses.”
“Other classes may prefer different activities; absent students were not represented.”
To plan for the whole school, gather broader, relevant responses before deciding.
focuses.watch: A graph alone is not a complete conclusion; explain its meaning in the investigation.
focuses.tryit: What would you change if many students selected “another activity”?
focuses.answer: Ask a follow-up neutral question to identify those activities, then revise categories and gather suitable evidence.

AC9M5P01.title: Equally and unequally likely outcomes
AC9M5P01.lead: List possible results systematically and use the chance setup to judge whether the results are equally likely.
AC9M5P01.before: Know a coin, die, spinner and drawing from a mixed collection.

focuses.title: Define what counts as an outcome
focuses.explain: An outcome is one possible recorded result. The same experiment can have different outcome lists depending on what is recorded.
focuses.example: Draw one card from a well-shuffled standard 52-card deck.
steps: Recording the exact card gives 52 possible outcomes.
Recording the suit gives four outcomes; recording its colour gives red or black.
These outcome descriptions answer different questions about the same draw.
focuses.watch: Do not mix exact cards and colours in one inconsistent outcome list.
focuses.tryit: List the outcomes when recording a fair six-sided die’s top number.
focuses.answer: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, each listed once.

focuses.title: Explain an equal-chance setup
focuses.explain: Equally likely means each specified outcome has the same chance. Justify it from the physical setup or stated fair model.
focuses.example: Draw one of five different names from a hat.
steps: Use one same-sized folded slip per person and mix the slips thoroughly.
With no way to favour a slip, each person has the same chance.
Two slips for one person would change the name chances even if every slip is mixed fairly.
focuses.watch: Possible does not mean equally likely. A random procedure can still produce unequal category chances.
focuses.tryit: A fair coin has which equally likely face outcomes?
focuses.answer: Heads and tails.

focuses.title: Distinguish individual objects from colour outcomes
focuses.explain: Individual matching counters can have equal chances while repeated colours have unequal chances. Spinner colour chances depend on the coloured shares of the whole.
focuses.example: Draw from a bag containing three red and one blue matching counter.
steps: There are four individual counters, with one blue opportunity and three red opportunities.
The possible colour results are red and blue, but red is more likely.
A fair spinner with four equal sectors, three red and one blue, models the same colour comparison.
focuses.watch: Two colour names do not create equal chances.
focuses.tryit: Four equal spinner sectors are red, red, blue and green. Which colour is most likely?
focuses.answer: Red, because two of the four equal sectors are red.

focuses.title: Judge fairness and keep evidence separate
focuses.explain: A game is fair between players when their winning rules give equal chances under the stated setup. A small run of wins does not prove the setup is biased.
focuses.example: On a fair die, one player wins on 1 or 2; another on 3, 4, 5 or 6.
steps: The first player has two equally likely number outcomes.
The second has four, so the rules favour the second player.
Giving each player three different numbers would balance their chances.
focuses.watch: Promotional collections or computer recommendations should not be assumed unbiased merely because several labels are possible; ask how selections are made.
focuses.tryit: Player A wins on odd and player B on even. Is this fair on a fair six-sided die?
focuses.answer: Yes: each has three equally likely number outcomes.

AC9M5P02.title: Repeated chance experiments
AC9M5P02.lead: Repeat a clear experiment, record every valid result and use frequencies to compare and estimate chances.
AC9M5P02.before: List possible outcomes and distinguish a predicted chance from a recorded result.

focuses.title: Set a repeatable protocol and predict
focuses.explain: A trial is one repetition. State what is recorded, how the setup stays consistent and how many trials you will perform.
focuses.example: Plan draws from a bag with three red and one blue matching counter.
steps: Predict red will occur more often because there are more red counters.
Draw without looking, record the colour, replace the counter and mix before the next draw.
Repeat 20 times and record every valid draw. Replacement keeps the same colour mix.
focuses.watch: Without replacement, later draws use a changed collection; it is a different experiment.
focuses.tryit: Why replace the counter after each draw in this plan?
focuses.answer: To keep three red and one blue counter available on every trial.

focuses.title: Conduct and record actual results
focuses.explain: Use a tally as each trial happens. Convert tallies to frequencies and check that the total equals the number of valid trials.
focuses.example: Read an illustrative 20-draw record: red 14, blue 6.
steps: 14 + 6 = 20, so the record accounts for all 20 draws.
Red occurred 14 out of 20 times; blue occurred 6 out of 20.
These are example data for learning. Your own actual 20 draws may differ.
focuses.watch: Do not discard an unexpected result to make the table fit a prediction.
focuses.tryit: Conduct your own 20 replacement draws. What must the two colour counts total?
focuses.answer: 20; keep and report the actual counts rather than copying the illustrative record.

focuses.title: Use relative frequency to estimate likelihood
focuses.explain: Relative frequency compares an outcome count with the total trial count. It allows comparison when experiment lengths differ.
focuses.example: Compare red 14 out of 20 with red 32 out of 40.
steps: The second record has a larger red proportion, even after accounting for its extra trials.
In a spreadsheet put counts 14 and 6 in B2:B3. =SUM(B2:B3) gives 20; =B2/SUM($B$2:$B$3) gives the red proportion.
focuses.watch: A larger raw count alone does not establish a greater relative frequency.
focuses.tryit: Which is the larger blue proportion: 5/20 or 8/40?
focuses.answer: 5/20 = 1/4 is larger than 8/40 = 1/5.

focuses.title: Compare setups and discuss variation
focuses.explain: Repeat both an equal-chance and an unequal-chance experiment. Compare their records with the physical setups and with other groups.
focuses.example: Compare a fair die labelled 1–6 with a fair cube labelled 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3.
steps: Each face is equally likely on either fair cube.
Number outcomes 1, 2 and 3 on the second cube are not equally likely: their face counts differ.
Roll each cube repeatedly, record number frequencies and compare. Larger trial totals can make proportions more informative but never guarantee exact expected counts.
focuses.watch: A short-run difference can be chance variation; it does not alone prove cheating or predict the next result.
focuses.tryit: Can ten fair coin tosses give seven heads?
focuses.answer: Yes. Equal long-run chances do not force an exact five–five split in ten trials.
